author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: Every few years, dry, cobweb-like Martian creatures ('buggies') drift down to Earth in clouds and are hunted and destroyed by panicked mobs the moment they are spotted.
page_summary:
Every few years, dry, cobweb-like Martian creatures ('buggies') drift down to Earth in clouds and are hunted and destroyed by panicked mobs the moment they are spotted. Ted Barnes comes home shaken after seeing one being pried off a neighbor's roof, and gives his eleven-year-old son Jimmy an urgent warning to run for help and never approach one. Walking home from school days later, Jimmy encounters a buggie clinging silently to a tree and, instead of an attack, receives a wordless telepathic vision of its dying home world and its people's desperate, humble request: permission merely to rest on the surface of Earth's oceans, drawing nutrients from the water, asking nothing more. Terrified, Jimmy runs for help anyway; a mob gathers, burns the creature out of the tree, and stomps it to death on the ground as it falls. The story ends at Ted's workplace, where he beams with pride retelling how brave and unafraid his son was — a pride the reader now knows is built on the fact that Jimmy alone, of everyone in the story, was shown unambiguous proof the buggies meant no harm, and reported them anyway.

**Why it matters.** The story's structure is quietly damning: by giving Jimmy full, unmediated access to the buggie's peaceful intentions before the mob kills it, Dick removes the usual science-fictional alibi of the 'first contact gone wrong through misunderstanding.' Nobody in this story misunderstands anything. The buggies are known, name and all ('buggies'), hunted on a known cycle, and killed by people who have simply decided, as an entire culture, that a harmless request for coexistence is not worth honoring. Jimmy's fear-driven betrayal of what he was shown is presented with more sympathy than judgment — he is a child raised inside a system of inherited terror — but the story's closing image of his father's oblivious pride turns the entire structure into an indictment of how atrocity gets absorbed into ordinary, celebrated life.

*Ted's repeated, satisfied 'Not a damn bit afraid' closes the story on willful ignorance rather than horror, letting the reader alone carry the knowledge of what was actually asked for, and refused.*

structure.form: short story in three movements: Ted's warning, Jimmy's encounter and betrayal of what he learns, and the story's ironic coda
movements: Ted arrives home shaken by a buggie sighting and instructs Jimmy never to approach one, only to report and flee.

Jimmy encounters a buggie directly, receives its telepathic plea to be allowed to live peacefully on the ocean's surface, and — despite understanding this — flees and summons a mob that burns and kills it.
At his office, Ted proudly retells the story of his son's courage, unaware that what actually happened was closer to a betrayal of a harmless, pleading creature than to bravery against a monster.
structure.point_of_view: third person, following Ted then Jimmy, with the telepathic vision rendered in unmediated sensory detail so the reader receives exactly what Jimmy receives — meaning the story deliberately withholds no information a more sympathetic response would have required.
structure.central_device: A direct telepathic transmission of the alien's own perspective and desperate, peaceful request, delivered in full to both Jimmy and the reader, so that the ensuing mob violence cannot be read as a tragic misunderstanding — everyone with access to the truth chooses fear and violence anyway.

characters.name: Jimmy Barnes
characters.note: The only character in the story given direct, unambiguous access to the buggie's peaceful intent, and the one who nonetheless runs for a mob rather than for mercy — his fear is presented sympathetically (he is a child acting exactly as his parents and school have trained him to) rather than as individual moral failure.

characters.name: Ted Barnes
characters.note: His closing scene of proud, oblivious boasting about his son's 'courage' is the story's sharpest irony — he is celebrating an act of successful, culturally-approved cruelty toward a being that had done nothing but ask for a small mercy.

characters.name: Lena Barnes
characters.note: Reinforces the culture of fear with a casual threat of physical punishment if Jimmy disobeys the warnings about the buggies, showing the mob response is instilled deliberately, generation to generation, rather than spontaneous.

characters.name: The buggie
characters.note: Explicitly gentle and desperate rather than threatening — its telepathic plea asks only to live, unharmed, on the ocean's surface, and it offers no resistance even as it is burned and beaten to death.

settings.name: The Barnes' suburban neighborhood
settings.note: An entirely ordinary American street and school-day setting, in which the periodic, ritualized hunting and killing of an alien species has become as unremarkable as any other seasonal event.

settings.name: Mars, seen through the buggie's transmitted memory
settings.note: A dying, withered world of failing machinery and dwindling population, rendered with unusual tenderness relative to the story's otherwise brisk pulp register.

motifs: A direct telepathic transmission that removes all ambiguity about the alien's peaceful intentions, making the ensuing violence a matter of choice rather than misunderstanding
A culture of inherited, ritualized fear passed from parent to child as practical safety instruction
A mob's casual cruelty ('Step on it!') treated by the story's other characters as ordinary civic action rather than atrocity
A father's proud retelling of an act of violence he does not know was, in fact, a betrayal of a harmless being's direct plea for mercy

distinctive_terms.label: Mind
distinctive_terms.note: The telepathic transmission is repeatedly described as entering Jimmy's mind directly, the story's central evidentiary device.

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick names this story in the same Exegesis list as 'Beyond the Door,' 'Of Withered Apples,' and 'The Eyes Have It' (all read in this project), cited immediately after his claim that only what comes in 'from outside' an illusory, self-generated world is genuinely real. The evidence-gathering script's automated title search missed this citation due to a capitalization mismatch between the corpus title ('Martians Come In Clouds') and the Exegesis's own rendering ('Martians Come in Clouds'); it is included here after direct verification of the source line.

evidence.source: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick
evidence.quote: "Martians Come in Clouds" "The Eyes Have It" "Beyond the Door" "Withered Apples" "Not by Its Cover"
evidence.reading: Grouped with four other early minor stories (all read in this project) as material Dick returned to decades later in support of his gnostic claim that reality only truly breaks in 'from outside' an illusory world — in this story, that intrusion would presumably be the buggie's telepathic transmission itself, an unmediated, truthful signal from an outside source that the story's human characters choose to destroy rather than receive.

open_questions: What does footnote 95 attached to the five-story Exegesis list actually say? Given this story's device of an unmediated 'signal from outside' being violently rejected, the footnote may bear directly on Dick's later Zebra/AI Voice concepts.
Is there secondary criticism reading this story as an early instance of Dick's recurring sympathy for the alien-as-victim, in contrast to more straightforward alien-invasion pulp of the same period?

Is the specific detail of the buggies wanting only to live on the ocean's surface (rather than land) ever connected by critics to later Dick works involving negotiated coexistence with nonhuman intelligences?

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.
